title: Efficient movement of plants through the various growth stages in the nursery

lessons.title: Growth stages and plant flow
lessons.html:
Plants on the move

In a production nursery, plants do not stay in one place. They move from propagation to growing on, to hardening off, to the sales or dispatch area. Each move should happen at the right time: too early and the plant may die or be set back; too late and it becomes root-bound, stretched or blocks space needed by the next batch.

Typical stages and moves

StageTypical locationReady to move when
Germination or rootingGermination room, mist houseSeedlings have true leaves or cuttings have rooted
WeaningShade house or less humid areaPlants cope with lower humidity without wilting
Plug or linerTunnel or shade houseRoots hold the plug together
Growing onTunnel or open blocksPlant reaches size and shape for the product
Hardening offOpen blocks in full sunPlant is tough enough for the customer's garden
DispatchSales or dispatch areaGraded, cleaned and labelled

Checking readiness

Readiness is judged on the plant, not only on the calendar. Tip out a few plugs or pots to check roots. Look at leaf number, colour and firmness. Use the production plan's expected dates as a guide, but report early if batches are ahead or behind.

Why efficient flow matters

Efficient movement keeps every structure working at full capacity, keeps plants growing without setbacks and ensures stock is ready when orders arrive. A full mist house of rooted cuttings that have not been moved out means no space for the next week's cuttings, and the whole plan slips.

lessons.title: Planning and carrying out plant moves
lessons.html:
Moving plants without losses

Plan the move

  • Check where the batch will go and that the space is clean, weeded and has working irrigation.
  • Check the weather: avoid moving tender plants into the open before frost or a heatwave without protection.
  • Arrange enough workers, trolleys and transport.
  • Tell the irrigation team so that the new block is watered on the correct programme.

Handle plants carefully

  • Water plants a few hours before moving so they are not stressed, but not so wet that trays are heavy and messy.
  • Lift trays and pots from underneath, not by stems or leaves.
  • Do not overload trolleys; secure tall plants so they do not fall over.
  • Move plants in the cooler part of the day where possible.
  • Water in after placing, if the plan requires it.

Keep identity and records

Labels must move with the batch. Update the stock record the same day: batch number, quantity moved, from where, to where, date, and any plants discarded. A batch that loses its label or record becomes a problem for order picking and traceability.

Gradual changes

Plants grown under mist, shade or in a tunnel must adjust to harsher conditions step by step. Moving rooted cuttings straight from mist into full sun can scorch and kill them. Follow the nursery's weaning and hardening-off steps.

Safety during moves

Moving plants involves lifting, pushing and sometimes vehicles. Lift with bent knees and a straight back, share heavy loads, keep paths clear, and only licensed, authorised drivers may operate tractors, forklifts or bakkies. Watch for wet, slippery floors in propagation areas.

lessons.title: Improving flow and using space well
lessons.html:
Keeping plants moving smoothly

Look ahead

Each week, check what batches are due to move in the next two to three weeks. Compare this with the space that will become free. If more plants are due to move than there is space for, warn the manager early so plans can be changed, extra space prepared or sales pushed.

Reduce handling

Every time a plant is picked up, it costs labour and risks damage. Reduce handling by:

  • Placing batches close to where they will go next.
  • Using Danish trolleys or trays that move many plants at once.
  • Spacing plants at the time of a move rather than as a separate job, where practical.
  • Laying out blocks in the same order as the growth stages.

Deal with slow and surplus stock

Some batches grow slowly or do not sell. They take up space and hide pests. Identify them on regular stock walks, and agree with the manager whether to grow them on, sell at a lower grade, use them as stock plants, or discard them. Do not let them block space for productive batches.

Track flow

  • Record the date each batch enters and leaves each stage.
  • Compare actual time in each stage with the planned time.
  • Note bottlenecks, such as a full hardening-off area.
  • Record losses during and after moves.

These records show where flow can improve, for example adding more weaning space or moving batches a week earlier.

Portfolio evidence

For this work-experience module, keep movement records, stock sheets, space plans and your mentor's comments as evidence of your work.

Key points

  • Move plants when they are ready, judged on the plant as well as the plan.
  • Prepare clean space with working irrigation before moving a batch.
  • Handle plants carefully and harden them off step by step.
  • Labels and stock records must move with every batch.
  • Look two to three weeks ahead and reduce unnecessary handling.
  • Lift safely and let only authorised drivers use vehicles.
